# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The museum occupied a former railway station in a town the railway had stopped visiting. Above its entrance, carved into stone, were the words ARRIVALS and DEPARTURES. Someone had installed the museum’s name between them on a modest wooden board, so that the whole building appeared to offer three possible conditions of existence.

ARRIVALS. THE MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS. DEPARTURES.

On wet mornings, rain traveled through the missing roof tiles and landed in a bucket beneath the old station clock. The clock had stopped at eleven seventeen. Visitors often assumed this was an exhibit.

“No,” said Ada, the curator. “That’s broken.”

They sometimes nodded as though she had said something profound.

The collection included a wedding dress with one sleeve, a chess game abandoned in 1963, the first nine chapters of a detective novel, and a wooden bird whose left wing remained trapped inside its original block.

There was a half-knitted yellow scarf. There was a map of an imaginary country whose coastline ended abruptly at a coffee stain. There was a letter beginning, *There is something I should have told you before.*

Nothing followed.

Ada had spent eleven years arranging these objects so they did not seem merely neglected. She believed there was a difference between a thing discarded and a thing held in suspension, although she had never found a satisfactory way to put that difference on a funding application.

Under “Public Benefit,” she usually wrote: *Preservation of local cultural material.*

The council seemed reassured by this.

***

Each donated object arrived with a form.

What is it?

Who began it?

Why was it not completed?

The third question caused trouble. People wrote *lack of time* when they meant divorce, *loss of interest* when they meant disappointment, and *circumstances* when they meant that the person who knew what came next had died.

Ada never corrected them.

Her favorite donation was a model sailing ship brought in by a retired dentist named Bell. It had a finished hull, three masts, and no rigging.

“I discovered,” he explained, “that I dislike string.”

He said it without embarrassment. Ada admired him enormously.

Other donors lingered. They touched the edge of a table or adjusted an object already sitting perfectly straight. One woman returned six times to visit an unfinished quilt, then stopped coming. A young man donated a screenplay and asked whether the museum could promise never to stage it.

“We don’t generally stage things,” Ada said.

“Yes, but could you promise?”

She did.

There were rules. The museum did not accept unpaid invoices, unresolved legal disputes, or living animals. It had once accepted a sourdough starter, but this created philosophical and practical difficulties.

Neither did it accept people.

That rule had been added after a man arrived carrying a folding chair and announced that he himself was the most important unfinished project in the county.

Ada offered him tea.

He stayed until closing, helped her bring in the pavement sign, and later became the museum’s accountant.

His name was Maurice.

***

The difficulty began with a chair.

It was a handsome oak chair, almost complete, except that one of its back legs was missing. Its maker had abandoned it after accepting a job in another city. A neighbor rescued it from a shed and brought it to the museum.

Ada displayed it on a low platform with a discreet support beneath the seat.

One Thursday, a girl named Nell visited with her school.

While the other children searched for answers on a worksheet, Nell crouched beside the chair.

“Why don’t you put the leg on?”

“Because then it wouldn’t be unfinished.”

“Would that be bad?”

“For this museum, it would be inconvenient.”

Nell considered this.

“Do you want things to stay wrong?”

Ada had developed answers to many questions. Was the missing sleeve lost? Had anyone finished reading the unfinished novel? Did the station clock work?

She had no prepared answer for this one.

“It isn’t always wrong for something to be unfinished,” she said.

“But that chair could be sat on.”

“Yes.”

“And nobody can sit on it now.”

“That’s true.”

Nell stood up. She looked neither victorious nor particularly interested in the damage she had done.

“My grandad makes legs,” she said.

“For furniture?”

“Mostly.”

Then her teacher called her away.

Ada remained beside the chair for several minutes. Eventually she straightened its label, although it was not crooked.

That evening, while locking up, she noticed how tired her own feet were. It was an irritating thing to notice.

***

The following week, the council sent a letter.

The museum’s grant would be reviewed in September. Attendance had declined. Heating costs had risen. The building required significant maintenance, particularly to its roof.

The council wished to see evidence of increased community engagement.

Maurice read the letter twice.

“They want more people.”

“We had more people last month.”

“How many?”

“Seventeen more.”

“Wasn’t there a school visit?”

“Yes.”

“How many children?”

“Twenty-three.”

He set the letter down.

Outside, wind pushed a crisp packet along the abandoned platform. It traveled several yards with apparent purpose, then caught beneath a bench.

“We could do an event,” Maurice said.

“We do events.”

“A different event.”

Their existing events included a lecture on abandoned canals, a reading of incomplete poems, and an annual evening at which local musicians performed movements from unfinished symphonies.

The symphony evening was poorly attended, but those who came were fiercely loyal.

“What sort of different event?”

Maurice hesitated.

“People could finish something.”

Ada looked at him.

“Not everything,” he added.

“You can’t invite people into a museum to dismantle its purpose.”

“Some museums let you grind flour.”

“They’re museums of milling.”

“Yes,” Maurice said. “I suppose those have an advantage. Milling is quite clear about what it wants.”

They sat in silence.

Rain began striking the bucket beneath the clock.

Maurice glanced toward it.

“Would fixing the roof count as vandalism?”

Ada tried not to smile. She failed, but only slightly.

“Put the kettle on,” she said.

***

That night, Ada walked through the galleries after closing.

Without visitors, the objects seemed less eager to explain themselves.

The yellow scarf lay in its case beside two knitting needles. Ada knew the donor’s story: a woman had begun it for her son before he moved to Canada. She had made it too wide, started again, grown annoyed, and bought him a coat instead.

He still lived in Canada. She still spoke to him every Sunday.

The scarf was not a tragedy. Ada had sometimes allowed visitors to think it was.

She stood before the wooden bird.

Its maker, a cabinetmaker recovering from a stroke, had carved it as an exercise. He stopped when movement returned sufficiently to his hand for him to repair a chest of drawers.

He had considered the bird a success.

Ada read her own label:

*An evocative study of arrested flight.*

For the first time, it struck her as rather rude.

In the office, she opened the donation records. Some objects had been given without conditions. Others were loans. A few carried explicit requests that they remain untouched.

She made three lists.

Things that must be preserved.

Things whose owners should be asked.

Things about which she knew too little.

The third list was longest.

At half past ten, she telephoned Maurice.

“I think,” she said, “we may have confused unfinished with waiting.”

He was quiet for a moment.

“Can we discuss this tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“Only I’m in the middle of something.”

***

Nell’s grandfather arrived wearing a green sweater dusted with pale curls of wood.

His name was Tomas. He carried a canvas tool bag and approached the chair with none of the reverence Ada had come to expect in the galleries.

He turned it upside down.

Ada made a small involuntary noise.

“Loose joint,” he said.

“The missing leg is the principal issue.”

“It has more than one issue.”

The chair’s original maker had replied to Ada’s letter with surprising speed.

*Please finish it. I never liked thinking of it in that shed.*

Tomas examined the surviving back leg. He measured it, sketched its profile, and asked whether the museum had a workbench.

It did not.

“Good table?”

“Yes.”

“One you don’t mind scratching?”

“No.”

He looked around.

“We’ll need to solve that first.”

The workbench came from the school. Clamps came from a plumber. A retired art teacher offered brushes, though nobody yet needed brushes. Someone donated a sewing machine, and someone else donated a second sewing machine because, apparently, the first had started a competition.

Ada called the event “A Weekend of Possible Completions.”

Maurice shortened it to “Finish Something” on the posters.

“Your version sounds uncertain,” he said.

“It is uncertain.”

“People can discover that when they arrive.”

They established rules. Permission mattered. Historical material would remain untouched. Nobody would finish another person’s letter. Nobody would be required to complete anything.

Ada insisted on the last rule.

Tomas nodded.

“Good. Some things are a bad idea.”

***

On Saturday morning, thirty-eight people were waiting outside.

Ada counted them through the office window, then counted again.

There were bicycles chained to the old railings. A woman held a lamp with a crooked shade. Two brothers carried a small table between them, arguing about which one had damaged it.

A man arrived with a cardboard box containing most of a radio.

“We said unfinished projects,” Ada told him. “Not necessarily repairs.”

“I started repairing it in 1998.”

She let him in.

By noon, the waiting room smelled of sawdust, warm electrical components, and tea.

Tomas worked on the chair while Nell sanded a piece of scrap wood beside him. Three women discussed the yellow scarf. Its donor had authorized them to unravel it if necessary, and they were approaching that possibility with the gravity of surgeons.

At the far end of the room, Maurice helped a teenager format a résumé.

“Is that an exhibit?” Ada asked.

“No,” he said. “But neither is the roof.”

Not everyone approved.

A regular visitor named Mrs. Vale stood before the empty chair platform.

“It looks like a jumble sale.”

“Only in the waiting room.”

“The atmosphere carries.”

Ada understood. She missed the quiet herself. Someone had put a mug on a display plinth. The plumber’s radio was receiving two stations at once.

Mrs. Vale looked toward the workbench.

“What happens when everything’s finished?”

“I don’t know,” Ada said.

This answer seemed to offend her more than the noise.

***

Near closing time, a woman named Ruth brought in a small blue cardigan.

She had begun it fourteen years earlier. The sleeves remained separate from the body, pinned into place with safety pins that had darkened at their hinges.

Ada recognized her from the library.

“Would you like someone to help sew it together?”

Ruth shook her head.

“I thought I would.”

They stood beside the sewing table. Around them, people were packing tools into boxes. One of the brothers had forgiven the other about the table, provisionally.

“It was for my daughter,” Ruth said.

Ada waited.

“She’s fourteen now. Perfectly healthy. Taller than I am.”

Ruth laughed, then pressed her lips together.

“I don’t know why I brought it.”

“To finish it, perhaps.”

“Perhaps.”

Ada drew out a chair.

Ruth sat with the cardigan across her knees.

After a while she said, “I think I wanted somebody to see that I did start.”

Ada sat beside her.

Across the room, Tomas fitted the chair’s new leg into its joint. Nell watched from the floor, solemnly holding a clamp she had been told not to tighten yet.

Ruth stroked one tiny cuff with her thumb.

“Could you keep it?”

“As it is?”

“Yes.”

“We could do that.”

“Not because anything terrible happened.”

“I’ll make sure the label says so.”

Ruth considered this.

“Could it just say I got busy?”

Ada brought her a donation form.

For the third question, Ruth wrote exactly that, in careful blue letters.

***

The chair was ready on Sunday afternoon.

Tomas placed it on the floor and stepped back.

Nobody sat down.

“Go on,” he told Ada.

She lowered herself cautiously onto the seat.

It held.

A small group applauded, which embarrassed her, though not enough to make her stand immediately. The chair was comfortable. Its back supported her at precisely the angle she liked.

The new leg was lighter than the others.

“We could stain it,” someone said.

“I’d rather not,” Ada replied.

Tomas nodded as though she had passed a test he had not mentioned.

By the end of the weekend, the scarf had become two narrow scarves. The radio received one station clearly. The table stood level. Three projects had been declared beyond rescue, and their owners seemed relieved.

Several others had barely progressed.

These, Ada discovered, had produced no less conversation.

Mrs. Vale returned on Sunday carrying a biscuit tin.

Inside was a collection of fabric squares.

“I’m not promising anything,” she said.

“No one’s asking you to.”

“I simply thought someone might know what sort of pattern this was meant to be.”

Ada directed her to the sewing table.

Later, Maurice counted the donations.

“Enough for the roof?”

“Enough for someone to look at the roof.”

“That’s a start.”

“Yes,” he said. “Though we should probably avoid collecting too many of those.”

They left the workbench in the waiting room. Moving it would have required six people, and all six had gone home.

***

In September, the council renewed the grant.

Not generously, but sufficiently.

The museum opened a workshop on the first Saturday of each month. Its collection continued to grow. People still brought things they wanted preserved, things they wanted released, and things whose meaning they hoped Ada could determine for them.

She became more careful about that last category.

The wooden bird received a new label. It described the cabinetmaker’s recovery and mentioned the chest of drawers.

The detective novel remained unfinished. Several visitors offered to write an ending, but the author’s daughter declined.

“He never knew who did it,” she explained. “I think he enjoyed that.”

Ruth’s cardigan went into a case beside the yellow scarves, one of which was eventually claimed by the donor for her granddaughter.

The other remained.

The chair stood near the entrance, available to anyone who needed it. Ada kept its old label in a drawer.

A roof repair silenced the bucket. Repairing the clock proved more expensive, so it continued to show eleven seventeen. When visitors asked, Ada still told them it was broken.

One afternoon, Nell arrived without her school.

She sat in the chair and swung her feet.

“Is it still in the museum?”

“Yes.”

“Even though it’s finished?”

“Yes.”

Nell examined the pale new leg.

“Good,” she said.

Then she took a book from her bag and began reading.

Ada returned to her desk. Outside, on the unused platform, Maurice was measuring the bench. One of its boards needed replacing.
